why_how.text: A title proves you own the vehicle, and buyers and new residents alike have thirty days to get one.
Titling also means paying the title fee, the larger processing fee and any sales taxes due.

scenario.text: Carlos buys a used pickup in Missouri and waits past thirty days to apply for the title.

reasoning.text: He had thirty days to go to a license office; missing that window after a purchase brings a penalty fee.

result.text: Carlos pays a penalty fee on top of the eight point five zero dollars title and the nine point zero zero dollars processing fee.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a new resident gets a longer titling window than a buyer.

correction.text: The same thirty-day window applies whether you just bought the vehicle or just became a Missouri resident.

memory_support.text: Thirty days to title, buyer or newcomer.

prompt.text: Nadia just moved to Missouri with a car she already owns. How long does she have to title it at a license office?

answer.text: Thirty days, the same window a buyer gets.

rationale.text: The same thirty-day titling window applies to buyers and to new residents.

lines.text: Thirty days to title.
A title proves ownership.
Fees, taxes and safe storage.

narration.text: This lesson is about titling a vehicle in Missouri, and it starts with a deadline. Whether you buy a vehicle as a Missouri resident or have just moved to Missouri, you have thirty days to go to a license office and title it. A title proves that you own the vehicle, so it matters to get it done inside that window, because applying late after a purchase brings a penalty fee. We will also look at what titling costs: the title fee, the processing fee and the sales taxes that are due. We finish with what happens after you apply, and where the title should be kept once it arrives in the mail.

lines.text: Buying as a Missouri resident: thirty days.
Just moved to Missouri: thirty days.
Title it at a license office.

narration.text: Start with the deadline itself. If you buy a vehicle while you live in Missouri, you have thirty days to go to a license office and title it. If you have just moved to Missouri and bring a vehicle with you, the window is exactly the same, thirty days. The guide stresses this point: the same thirty-day window applies to titling whether you just bought the vehicle or just became a Missouri resident. So you do not need to remember two different titling deadlines for these two situations. A recent buyer and a recent newcomer both head to a license office within thirty days to title the vehicle.

lines.text: A title proves you own the vehicle.
Apply within thirty days of buying.
Late after a purchase: penalty fee.

narration.text: Why does the deadline matter so much? A title is the document that proves you own the vehicle. The guide attaches a cost to waiting: if you do not apply for the title within thirty days of buying the vehicle, you must pay a penalty fee. Picture a buyer who picks up a car and then lets the weeks slide past the thirty-day mark. When that buyer finally goes to a license office, the title still has to be applied for, and now a penalty fee is added on top of the usual charges. Applying inside the thirty days is how a buyer gets proof of ownership without paying that penalty fee.

lines.text: Apply at any license office.
Title: eight point five zero dollars.
Processing fee: nine point zero zero dollars.

narration.text: Now the costs. You can apply for a title at any license office, so you are not tied to one location. The title itself costs eight point five zero dollars. There is also a processing fee of nine point zero zero dollars charged along with it. These are two separate charges, and the title fee is not the only amount you pay at the counter when you apply. Both of them are owed together at the time you apply for the title. On the next slide we look closely at these two amounts, because they are close enough in size to swap by accident, and a question may test exactly which charge is which.

lines.text: Title fee: the smaller charge.
Processing fee: the larger charge.
Do not swap the two amounts.

narration.text: Here is the trap. The title fee and the processing fee are close in size, so it is easy to swap them. The title itself costs eight point five zero dollars, while the processing fee charged with it is nine point zero zero dollars. That makes the processing fee the larger of the two. If a question offers a title at nine point zero zero dollars with an eight point five zero dollars processing fee, the amounts have been reversed. One way to hold it is that the fee for processing the paperwork is larger than the fee for the title itself. Check which charge each amount belongs to before you choose an answer.

lines.text: Pay all state and local sales taxes due.
Ask any license office.
Or use the online sales tax calculator.

narration.text: Fees are not the whole bill. When you title a vehicle, you must also pay all the state and local sales taxes that are due. Notice the word all: the guide covers both state and local taxes, not just one of them. If you want to know the amount before you go, information on sales tax due can be obtained from any license office or from the Department's online sales tax calculator. So a buyer planning a trip to the license office can check the sales tax first, then arrive ready to pay the title fee, the processing fee and the sales taxes that are due, all at the time of titling.

lines.text: Nadia moved to Missouri last week.
She brought a car she already owns.
How long does she have to title it?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Nadia moved to Missouri last week and brought along a car she already owns. A friend tells her that newcomers get a longer titling window than people who buy a car here. How long does Nadia have to go to a license office and title her car? Work it out before reading on. The answer is thirty days. Whether you buy a vehicle as a Missouri resident or have just moved to Missouri, you have thirty days to title it. The same thirty-day window applies to titling for a buyer and for a new resident, so the friend is wrong, and Nadia gets no extra time.

lines.text: You get a receipt when you apply.
The Department mails the title later.
Keep the title out of your vehicle.

narration.text: To close, follow the title after you apply. You receive a receipt when you apply at the license office, and the Department later mails you the title. So walking out with only a receipt is normal; the title itself comes by mail. Once it arrives, think about where you keep it. A title is an important personal document, so do not keep it in your vehicle. Tie that back to the start of the lesson: the title proves that you own the vehicle, which is exactly why it deserves a place outside the car. Title within thirty days, pay the fees and taxes, then store the mailed title away from the vehicle.

why_how.text: Title requirements differ for new and used vehicles and for in-state and out-of-state purchases, so the new Missouri purchase has its own papers.
The MSO shows the vehicle is new and never registered, and it carries the odometer disclosure.

scenario.text: Maya buys a new car from a Missouri dealer.

reasoning.text: A new vehicle bought in Missouri comes with a title application and an assigned MSO, which shows it was never registered.

result.text: Maya and the dealer fill in the odometer disclosure on the back of the MSO.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a new car's odometer reading goes on the back of a title.

correction.text: For a new vehicle, you and the dealer fill in the odometer disclosure on the back of the MSO.

memory_support.text: New car, MSO carries the miles.

prompt.text: Maya buys a brand-new car from a Missouri dealer. Which two documents does the dealer give her, and what does one of them show?

answer.text: A title application and an assigned MSO; the MSO shows the car is new and never registered.

rationale.text: For a new vehicle bought in Missouri the dealer supplies both, and the MSO shows the vehicle is new.

lines.text: Requirements change with the purchase.
New Missouri vehicle: application and MSO.
Odometer goes on the MSO.

narration.text: This lesson covers the paperwork for a brand-new vehicle bought in Missouri. Title requirements are not the same for every purchase. They differ for new and used vehicles, and for vehicles bought inside or outside Missouri, so the first question to ask is always which kind of purchase you made. Here we take the new vehicle bought from a Missouri dealer. The dealer gives you a title application and an assigned Manufacturer's Statement of Origin, called the MSO. We will see what the MSO shows, and where the odometer reading for a new vehicle is written, which is on the MSO rather than on a title.

lines.text: New or used vehicle.
Bought inside or outside Missouri.
Each mix has its own papers.

narration.text: Before any document, sort the purchase. The guide says title requirements differ for new and used vehicles and for vehicles bought inside or outside Missouri. That gives you two questions to answer. First, is the vehicle new or used? Second, did you buy it in Missouri or in another state? A new vehicle from a Missouri dealer, a used vehicle from a Missouri seller, a new vehicle from an out-of-state dealer and a used vehicle bought out of state each come with their own set of papers. This lesson follows the first case, the new vehicle bought in Missouri, and the next lessons take the other cases in turn.

lines.text: A title application.
An assigned MSO.
MSO: new, never registered.

narration.text: When you buy a new vehicle in Missouri, the dealer gives you two things for titling: a title application and an assigned Manufacturer's Statement of Origin, or MSO. The MSO has a specific job. It shows that the vehicle is new and has never been registered. That fits the guide's contrast between the two kinds of vehicle: a new vehicle comes with an MSO from the dealer, while a used vehicle comes with a properly assigned title from the seller. So if you are holding a title application and an assigned MSO from a Missouri dealer, you have the documents the guide describes for a new vehicle bought in the state.

lines.text: New vehicle: disclosure on the MSO back.
You and the dealer fill it in.
Not on a title.

narration.text: Here is the trap with new vehicles. Many mileage questions are really about titles, but the new-vehicle rule points somewhere else. For a new vehicle, you and the dealer fill in the odometer disclosure on the back of the MSO. Put another way, the odometer reading goes on the MSO rather than on a title. If an answer choice says the reading for a brand-new car goes on the back of a title, it is describing a different situation. Keep two details together for a new vehicle: the place is the back of the MSO, and the people who fill it in are you and the dealer, not the dealer alone and not you alone.

lines.text: Maya buys a new car in Missouri.
The dealer hands her two papers.
What are they, and what does one show?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Maya buys a brand-new car from a dealer in Missouri. Before she heads to a license office to title it, the dealer hands her two documents. What are those two documents, and what does one of them show about her car? Work it out before reading on. The dealer gives her a title application and an assigned Manufacturer's Statement of Origin, or MSO. The MSO shows that the vehicle is new and has never been registered. Because her car is new, it comes with an MSO from the dealer rather than a properly assigned title from a seller, which is what a used vehicle would come with.

lines.text: Title application from the dealer.
Assigned MSO from the dealer.
Odometer disclosure on the MSO back.

narration.text: To close, put the new-vehicle steps in order. First, recognize the kind of purchase, because title requirements differ for new and used vehicles and for vehicles bought inside or outside Missouri. Second, for a new vehicle bought in Missouri, collect the title application and the assigned MSO from the dealer. Third, remember what the MSO shows: the vehicle is new and has never been registered. Fourth, you and the dealer fill in the odometer disclosure on the back of the MSO, so the reading goes on the MSO rather than on a title. With those papers in hand, the new Missouri vehicle is ready to be titled at a license office.

why_how.text: A used vehicle bought in Missouri changes hands through a properly assigned title, not an MSO.
The assigned title carries the sale details and, for newer vehicles, the mileage that both parties confirm.

scenario.text: Theo sells his used car, model year two thousand eleven or newer and under twenty years old, to a private buyer.

reasoning.text: The seller must give a properly assigned title, and under the odometer rule the seller writes the mileage on the assignment.

result.text: Theo writes the mileage, and both he and the buyer print and sign their names to confirm it.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a used vehicle comes with an MSO, just like a new one.

correction.text: A new vehicle comes with an MSO from the dealer, while a used vehicle comes with a properly assigned title from the seller.

memory_support.text: Used car, seller writes the miles.

prompt.text: Theo sells a used car of model year two thousand eleven or newer that is under twenty years old. Who writes the mileage, and where?

answer.text: Theo, the seller, writes it on the title assignment.

rationale.text: The disclosure rule covers model year two thousand eleven and newer until twenty years old, and the seller records the mileage.

lines.text: Used Missouri vehicle: assigned title.
What the title must list.
Who records the mileage.

narration.text: This lesson moves from new vehicles to used ones bought in Missouri. For a used vehicle, the seller must give you a properly assigned title, and if the seller is a dealer, the dealer should also give you a completed title application. We will contrast that with the MSO that comes with a new vehicle, walk through everything a properly assigned title lists, and then cover odometer disclosure. That rule depends on the model year: vehicles of model year two thousand eleven and newer need it on the back of the title until the vehicle is twenty years old. We finish with how the buyer and seller confirm the mileage together.

lines.text: Seller gives a properly assigned title.
Dealer seller adds a title application.
Applies to used vehicles bought in Missouri.

narration.text: Start with the used vehicle bought in Missouri. The seller must give you a properly assigned title. That is a must, whether the seller is a private person or a dealer. When the seller is a dealer, there is one more piece: the dealer should also give you a completed title application. So a buyer from a private seller walks away with the properly assigned title, and a buyer from a dealer walks away with the properly assigned title plus a completed title application. In both cases the assigned title is the key document, and the next slides look at what a properly assigned title lists and how it differs from the MSO.

lines.text: New vehicle: MSO from the dealer.
Used vehicle: assigned title from the seller.
Match the paper to the vehicle.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Two documents can look like they do the same job, and questions like to swap them. A new vehicle comes with an MSO from the dealer, while a used vehicle comes with a properly assigned title from the seller. The MSO shows that a vehicle is new and has never been registered, so it does not fit a used vehicle. A used vehicle bought in Missouri comes with a properly assigned title from its seller. When a question describes a used car and offers an MSO, or describes a new car and offers an assigned title from the last owner, the papers have been mismatched. Match the paper to whether the vehicle is new or used.

lines.text: Buyer's name and address.
Odometer reading if needed, price, date.
Any lienholder; seller signatures and names.
Buyer's printed name and signature if needed.

narration.text: What does a properly assigned title show? The guide gives a full list. It shows the buyer's name and address. It shows the odometer reading if one is needed. It shows the sale price and the sale date. It names any lienholder. It carries every seller's signature and printed name, so if more than one person is selling, each one signs and prints. Finally, it shows the buyer's printed name and signature if needed. One way to walk through it is: who is buying, what the mileage is, what was paid and when, who holds a lien, and who is selling. Each of these items appears on a properly assigned title.

lines.text: Model year two thousand eleven and newer.
Disclosure until twenty years old.
Seller writes the mileage.

narration.text: Now odometer disclosure on used vehicles. An odometer disclosure on the back of the title is required for vehicles of model year two thousand eleven and newer, until the vehicle is twenty years old. So two conditions apply together: the model year must be two thousand eleven or newer, and the vehicle must be under twenty years old. When a vehicle that meets both conditions is sold, the seller writes the mileage on the title assignment. Compare this with a new vehicle, where you and the dealer fill in the disclosure on the back of the MSO. For a used vehicle under the rule, the place is the title assignment and the writer is the seller.

lines.text: Theo sells his used car.
It falls under the odometer rule.
Who writes the mileage, and where?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Theo is selling a used car of model year two thousand eleven or newer, and it is still under twenty years old. The buyer has the properly assigned title in front of her and asks who should fill in the mileage. Who writes the mileage, and on what part of the paperwork? Work it out before reading on. Theo, as the seller, writes the mileage on the title assignment. An odometer disclosure on the back of the title is required for vehicles of model year two thousand eleven and newer until they are twenty years old. After that, both the buyer and the seller print and sign their names to confirm the mileage.

lines.text: Buyer and seller print and sign.
Sometimes a separate odometer statement.
Used: assigned title; new: MSO.

narration.text: To close, finish the mileage step. Both the buyer and the seller print and sign their names to confirm the mileage, and sometimes a separate odometer statement is needed as well. So the seller writes the mileage, but confirming it is a two-person job. Pull the lesson together. A used vehicle bought in Missouri comes with a properly assigned title from the seller, plus a completed title application when the seller is a dealer. That title lists the buyer, the mileage if needed, the price, the date, any lienholder and the signatures. For model year two thousand eleven and newer under twenty years old, the mileage goes on the title assignment.

why_how.text: Out-of-state purchases need different papers depending on whether the vehicle is new or used.
A title from another state also needs an ID or OD form that only a licensed inspection station completes.

scenario.text: Rosa buys a used car from a private seller in another state that issues titles.

reasoning.text: She needs a properly assigned title from the seller, and because that title is from another state, an ID or OD form.

result.text: Rosa takes the car to a licensed inspection station to complete the ID or OD form.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking any license office clerk can complete the ID or OD form for every used car.

correction.text: The form is needed only for a title issued by another state, and only a licensed inspection station can complete it.

prompt.text: Rosa buys a used car in another state and is assigned that state's title. Which extra form does she need, and who completes it?

answer.text: An ID or OD verification form, completed by a licensed inspection station.

rationale.text: The form is needed only for a title issued by another state, and only a licensed inspection station can complete it.

lines.text: New from an out-of-state dealer.
Used: assigned or reassigned title.
Other-state titles need an ID or OD form.

narration.text: This lesson covers vehicles bought outside Missouri. The papers depend on whether the vehicle is new or used. A new vehicle bought out of state needs the dealer's invoice or a bill of sale plus the assigned MSO from that dealer. A used vehicle bought out of state needs a properly assigned title from the seller or a reassigned title from the dealer. We will also cover the state that does not require a title at all, the identification number and odometer verification form that a title from another state calls for, and the separate rules for a vehicle bought for salvage, dismantling or rebuilding.

lines.text: Dealer's invoice or a bill of sale.
Plus the assigned MSO.
The MSO comes from that dealer.

narration.text: Start with a new vehicle bought out of state. You need two kinds of paper. The first is either the dealer's invoice or a bill of sale. The second is the assigned MSO from that dealer, the same kind of document that shows a vehicle is new and has never been registered. Compare this with a new vehicle bought in Missouri, where the dealer gives you a title application and an assigned MSO. In both cases the MSO travels with the new vehicle. What changes out of state is the other paper: the dealer's invoice or a bill of sale goes along with the assigned MSO from the dealer who sold you the vehicle.

lines.text: Properly assigned title from the seller.
Or a reassigned title from the dealer.
Dealer reassigns; private seller assigns.

narration.text: Next, a used vehicle bought out of state. You need a properly assigned title from the seller or a reassigned title from the dealer. The difference is who is passing the title along. Out of state, a used vehicle may come with a reassigned title from a dealer instead of a title assigned by a private seller. Either way, the paper you need is a title, not an MSO, because the vehicle is used. So if you buy from a private person in another state, look for a properly assigned title. If you buy from a dealer in another state, a reassigned title from that dealer meets the requirement the guide describes for this case.

lines.text: Some states do not require a title.
Bring a bill of sale.
And the last certificate of registration.

narration.text: Some states do not require a title for the vehicle at all. In that case there is no title for the seller to assign, so the guide asks for two other papers. You need a bill of sale and the vehicle's last certificate of registration from that state. The certificate has to be the last one, from the state where you bought the vehicle. A buyer who comes back from such a state with only a bill of sale has just one of the two papers the guide lists. Compare this with a used vehicle from a state that does use titles, where you need a properly assigned title from the seller or a reassigned title from the dealer.

title.text: Who completes the ID or OD

lines.text: Needed only for an other-state title.
Only a licensed inspection station completes it.
Not the buyer, seller or clerk.

narration.text: Here is the trap. If the title assigned to you is from another state, a licensed inspection station must complete an identification number and odometer verification form, known as the ID or OD form. Two limits make this easy to get wrong. The form is needed only when the title assigned to you was issued by another state, so a title from Missouri assigned to you does not call for it. And only a licensed inspection station can complete it, not the seller, not the buyer and not a license office clerk. If an answer says anyone else fills in the ID or OD form, or that every used vehicle needs one, it does not match the guide.

lines.text: Rosa buys a used car elsewhere.
The seller assigns that state's title.
What form is needed, and who completes it?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Rosa buys a used car from a private seller in another state. The seller hands her a properly assigned title that was issued by that other state, and Rosa brings it home to Missouri to title the car. Which extra form does she need, and who is allowed to complete it? Work it out before reading on. She needs an identification number and odometer verification form, the ID or OD form, because the title assigned to her is from another state. Only a licensed inspection station can complete it. The form is needed only when the assigned title was issued by another state, which is exactly Rosa's situation.

lines.text: Salvage, dismantling or rebuilding.
Separate rules apply.
Ask the Motor Vehicle Bureau.

narration.text: To close, one case sits outside everything in this lesson. Titling a vehicle bought for salvage, dismantling or rebuilding has separate rules, and the guide points you to the Motor Vehicle Bureau for them. The steps we covered are for other purchases. A new vehicle from another state needs the dealer's invoice or a bill of sale plus the assigned MSO. A used vehicle needs a properly assigned title from the seller or a reassigned title from the dealer. A vehicle from a state with no title needs a bill of sale and the last certificate of registration. And a title assigned to you from another state needs an ID or OD form from a licensed inspection station.

why_how.text: Missouri residents must register here, and a new resident's thirty-day registration deadline is separate from the titling window.
Registration brings plates with a year tab, a fee set by the vehicle, and a one-year or two-year term set by parity.

scenario.text: Jun moves to Missouri in an even-numbered year with a car whose model year is odd.

reasoning.text: He must register within thirty days of becoming a resident, and his parities do not match.

result.text: Jun registers within thirty days and is offered a one-year registration.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a new resident's registration deadline is the same thing as the titling window.

correction.text: Registration has its own thirty-day deadline, counted from the day you become a Missouri resident.

prompt.text: In an even-numbered year, Jun registers a car with an odd model year. Can he register it for two years?

answer.text: No; only one year is offered because the parities do not match.

rationale.text: Two years needs matching parity, such as an even model year in an even-numbered year.

lines.text: Residents register in Missouri.
New residents: thirty days.
Plates, fees and term length.

narration.text: This lesson turns from titles to registration. Missouri residents must register their vehicles in Missouri, and a new resident must do so within thirty days of moving in. We will look at how that registration deadline is counted, what a new resident does with an out-of-state title, including the case where a lender holds it, and what registering gets you, which is Missouri license plates with a year tab. Then we cover how the registration fee is set, when a two-year registration is possible under the parity rule, and the option of personalized or specialty plates, which can carry an extra fee.

lines.text: Residents must register in Missouri.
New residents: within thirty days.
Counted from the day you become a resident.

narration.text: Start with the rule. Missouri residents must register their vehicles in Missouri. A new resident must do so within thirty days of moving in. The guide is specific about when that clock starts: registration of a new resident's vehicle has its own thirty-day deadline, counted from the day you become a Missouri resident. So the starting point is not the day you buy a vehicle or the day an old registration runs out. It is the day you become a resident. A family that moves to Missouri counts thirty days from that day to get their vehicles registered, and they can register at any license office.

lines.text: Titling window: thirty days.
Registration deadline: its own thirty days.
Count registration from residency.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A new resident faces two deadlines that are both thirty days long, and they are easy to blur into one. The same thirty-day window applies to titling whether you just bought the vehicle or just became a Missouri resident. Registration of a new resident's vehicle has its own thirty-day deadline, counted from the day you become a Missouri resident. Both are thirty days, but they are two separate requirements: one for the title and one for the registration. When a question asks about registration, look for the deadline counted from the day you became a resident, and do not mix it up with the titling window.

lines.text: Turn in the out-of-state title.
Apply for a Missouri title.
Lender holds it? Statement plus one document.

narration.text: Registering as a new resident goes hand in hand with titling. A new resident must turn in the out-of-state title and apply for a Missouri title. Sometimes the title cannot be turned in, because a lender holds the out-of-state title and cannot release it. In that case, you provide a statement from the lender saying it will not surrender the title, plus one of three supporting documents. So the lender's statement alone is not enough; one of the three supporting documents has to go with it. The usual path is to hand in the out-of-state title, and the lender path is the exception for a title that the lender holds and cannot release.

lines.text: Registration brings plates with a year tab.
Passenger fee: taxable horsepower.
Commercial fee: zone and gross weight.

narration.text: What does registering get you? Registering your vehicle gets you Missouri license plates with a year tab on the plate. You can register at any license office. The fee is not one flat amount. For a passenger vehicle, the fee depends on its taxable horsepower. For a commercial vehicle, it depends on its zone and gross weight. On top of that, a processing fee is added. So a passenger car and a commercial vehicle have their fees set by different measures. If a question asks what sets a passenger car's fee, the answer is taxable horsepower, plus the processing fee; zone and gross weight belong to commercial vehicles.

lines.text: Parity must match for two years.
Even model year, even-numbered year.
Odd model year, odd-numbered year.
Otherwise, only one year.

narration.text: Registration length depends on parity, meaning whether a number is even or odd. A two-year registration is possible when the year parity matches: an even model year in an even-numbered year, or an odd model year in an odd-numbered year. Otherwise only one year is offered. The guide gives an example. In an even-numbered year such as two thousand eighteen, a vehicle with an even model year can be registered for two years. Following the same rule, an odd model year in that even-numbered year does not match, so only one year would be offered. Check the parity of the model year against the parity of the current year.

lines.text: It is an even-numbered year.
Jun's car has an odd model year.
How long can Jun register it?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: it is an even-numbered year, and Jun is registering a car whose model year is odd. He would like the longer two-year registration so he can skip next year's trip to the license office. Can Jun register his car for two years, or only for one? Work it out before reading on. The answer is only one year. A two-year registration is possible when the year parity matches, an even model year in an even-numbered year or an odd model year in an odd-numbered year. Jun's odd model year does not match the even-numbered year, so only one year is offered to him.

lines.text: Personalized or specialty plates are allowed.
An extra plate fee can apply.
It sits on top of the normal fee.

narration.text: To close, a word on plate choices. Registration gets you Missouri license plates with a year tab, but you are not limited to standard plates. You may choose personalized or specialty plates, which can carry an extra personalized plate fee on top of the normal registration fee. So the choice adds to the bill rather than replacing the normal fee. Pull the lesson together: residents register in Missouri, a new resident has thirty days counted from the day of becoming a resident, the out-of-state title is turned in, the fee depends on horsepower or zone and weight plus processing, and two years needs matching parity.

why_how.text: The renewal notice should come about two months ahead, but renewing on time is required either way.
Renewal papers depend on your situation, from tax receipts by registration term to an inspection certificate if one applies.

scenario.text: Lucia's last registration ran two years, and her notice lists a tax receipt and an inspection certificate.

reasoning.text: After a two-year registration she shows receipts for both previous years, and the certificate must be from the last sixty days.

result.text: She brings both tax receipts and a certificate from the last sixty days.

claim.text: Common mistake: waiting for the renewal notice before renewing.

correction.text: The notice should arrive about two months ahead, but you must renew on time even if it never comes.

prompt.text: Lucia's last registration ran for two years. Is last year's tax receipt enough for her renewal?

answer.text: No; after a two-year registration she shows receipts for both previous years.

rationale.text: One receipt fits a one-year registration; a two-year registration needs receipts for both years.

lines.text: Notice arrives about two months ahead.
Renew on time regardless.
Bring what your notice lists.

narration.text: This lesson covers renewing your registration. A renewal notice should arrive by mail about two months before your registration expires, but you must renew your plates on time even if it never comes. We will look at keeping your address current so the notice reaches you, the papers renewal can require, including tax receipts that depend on whether your last registration ran one year or two, proof of financial responsibility, and the inspection certificate window. Not every item on the renewal list applies to every owner, so we will also see why you read your own notice, and how a PIN on that notice can let you renew online.

lines.text: Notice by mail, about two months early.
No notice? Still renew on time.
Moved? Update your address.

narration.text: Start with the renewal notice. It should arrive by mail about two months before your registration expires. The key word is should. If the notice never comes, you must still renew your plates on time, so a missing notice is not a reason to let the registration lapse. To be sure your renewal notice reaches you, update your address whenever you move. You can report an address change by email with your full name, your old and new addresses, your driver license number or the last four digits of your Social Security number, and your plate numbers. Keeping the address current is how the notice finds you.

lines.text: The renewal notice.
Last year's receipt or a title copy.
Tax receipt or non-assessment statement.
Check your own notice's list.

narration.text: What do you bring? To renew you may need the renewal notice, last year's registration receipt or a copy of your title, plus a paid personal property tax receipt or a statement of non-assessment. That tax receipt comes from the county where you live, or from the city of St. Louis, for the period of your previous registration. Notice the word may. Not every item on the renewal list applies to every owner, so read the list on your own renewal notice and bring what it asks for. Set the notice beside your papers and match each item it lists against what you have before you go to the license office.

lines.text: One-year registration: last year's receipt.
Two-year registration: both previous years.
From your county or St. Louis.

narration.text: The tax receipt you show depends on how long your last registration ran. After a one-year registration you show last year's tax receipt. After a two-year registration you show receipts for both previous years. So the number of receipts follows the length of the registration you are renewing. Each one is a paid personal property tax receipt from the county where you live, or from the city of St. Louis, covering the period of your previous registration. The renewal list also allows a statement of non-assessment in place of a paid receipt. Before you renew, check how long your last registration ran, then gather a receipt for each year of it.

lines.text: Current insurance card or other proof.
Correct registration and processing fee.
Inspection certificate from the last sixty days.

narration.text: Three more items can be on your list. Renewal may require a current insurance card or other proof of financial responsibility. It may require the correct registration and processing fee. And if an inspection applies to your vehicle, renewal needs a safety and or emissions inspection certificate from the last sixty days. Notice the condition on that last item: it applies only if an inspection applies to your vehicle. When it does, the certificate has to be recent, from within the last sixty days, so an older certificate does not meet the rule. Put the insurance proof, the fee and any needed certificate beside the notice and tax papers before you go.

lines.text: Notice: about two months ahead.
Inspection certificate: last sixty days.
Different clocks, different directions.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Two time spans in renewal sound alike. The renewal notice comes about two months ahead of expiration, but the inspection certificate you bring must be from within the last sixty days. One looks forward: the notice should arrive about two months before your registration expires. The other looks back: the certificate must be from within the last sixty days. If an answer ties the certificate to the day the notice arrived, or lets a certificate be any age, it has mixed up the two rules. Keep them apart. The two months are about when the notice should arrive, and the sixty days are about how recent the certificate must be.

lines.text: Lucia's last registration ran two years.
She is renewing now.
Which tax receipts does she show?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Lucia registered her car for two years last time, and her renewal notice has just arrived. She finds last year's paid personal property tax receipt in her files and thinks that is all she needs for the tax part of her renewal. Is one receipt enough, or does she need more? Work it out before reading on. Lucia needs more. After a one-year registration you show last year's tax receipt, but after a two-year registration you show receipts for both previous years. Her receipts come from the county where she lives, or the city of St. Louis, for the period of her previous registration.

lines.text: You may be able to renew online.
If you qualify, a PIN is on your notice.
Read your own notice's list.

narration.text: To close, one more reason the notice matters. You may be able to renew your plates online, and if you qualify, a PIN is printed on your renewal notice. So the same notice that should arrive about two months ahead can also tell you whether online renewal is open to you. Pull the lesson together. Renew on time even without a notice, and update your address whenever you move. Bring what your own notice lists, which may include a prior receipt or title copy, the tax receipt or non-assessment statement, proof of financial responsibility, the correct fees, and an inspection certificate from the last sixty days if one applies.

How a plate went missing decides the cost: stolen means only the processing fee, lost or destroyed means a fee plus processing.

rationale.text: The per-plate charge is for lost or destroyed plates; stolen ones with an affidavit cost only the processing fee.

lines.text: Selling: Notice of Sale.
Lost or destroyed: apply to replace.
Stolen: affidavit and processing fee.

narration.text: This final lesson covers two situations: selling a vehicle, and replacing plates, tabs or a title. State law requires you to report selling a motor vehicle or all-terrain vehicle with a Notice of Sale, Form five thousand forty-nine, within thirty days. We will see where that form can be turned in. Then we look at replacements. If your plates, tabs or title are lost or destroyed, you are required to apply for a replacement, and each item has a cost. Stolen plates and tabs are handled differently, with a notarized affidavit, a limit of two times a year, and nothing to pay beyond the processing fee.

lines.text: Report a sale within thirty days.
Form five thousand forty-nine.
Any license office, or by mail.

narration.text: Start with selling. State law requires you to report selling a motor vehicle or all-terrain vehicle with a Notice of Sale, Form five thousand forty-nine, within thirty days. Notice that the rule covers all-terrain vehicles as well as motor vehicles, and that the duty is on the person who sells. The Notice of Sale can be turned in at any license office or mailed to the address printed on the form, so a seller has two ways to file it. Compare this with the buyer's side of the same sale, where the buyer has thirty days to go to a license office and title the vehicle. Both sides have thirty days, for two different tasks.

lines.text: Lost or destroyed? You must replace it.
Title: eight point five zero dollars.
Each plate or set of tabs: same price.
Plus a nine point zero zero dollars processing fee.

narration.text: Next, replacements. If your plates, tabs or title are lost or destroyed, you are required to apply for a replacement, so this is not optional. Replacing a lost or destroyed title costs eight point five zero dollars. Plates cost eight point five zero dollars per plate, so the price counts each plate. A set of tabs costs eight point five zero dollars. Each of these comes with a nine point zero zero dollars processing fee on top. Notice that a replacement title costs the same eight point five zero dollars as the title fee when you first titled the vehicle, and the processing fee is again the larger of the two charges.

lines.text: Notarized affidavit that they were stolen.
Up to two times a year.
Only the processing fee.

narration.text: Stolen plates and tabs follow a different rule. With a notarized affidavit that they were stolen, you can replace stolen plates and tabs up to two times a year at no cost apart from a nine point zero zero dollars processing fee. Three conditions come together here. The affidavit must be notarized and must say the plates and tabs were stolen. The free replacement for stolen plates and tabs is limited to two times per year. And the processing fee still applies, so free means no replacement charge rather than nothing at all. A driver with an affidavit, within the yearly limit, pays only the processing fee for stolen plates and tabs.

lines.text: Stolen: only the processing fee.
Lost or destroyed: a fee plus processing.
Ask how the item went missing.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Questions about replacement costs hinge on how the plate or tab went missing. Stolen plates and tabs are replaced at no charge beyond the nine point zero zero dollars processing fee, while lost or destroyed ones cost eight point five zero dollars each plus that fee. So a stolen plate with a notarized affidavit costs only the processing fee, and a lost plate costs eight point five zero dollars plus the processing fee. If a choice charges the full replacement price for stolen plates, or offers lost plates for the processing fee alone, the two cases have been swapped. Ask first whether the item was stolen, or lost or destroyed.

lines.text: Owen's plates were stolen.
He has a notarized affidavit.
What does he pay, and how often?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Owen's license plates were stolen from his car, and he has a notarized affidavit saying so. This is the first time this year it has happened to him. He expects to pay eight point five zero dollars for each plate plus the processing fee. Is he right, and how many times a year does this kind of replacement work? Work it out before reading on. Owen is not right. With a notarized affidavit, stolen plates and tabs are replaced at no cost apart from the nine point zero zero dollars processing fee, up to two times a year. The eight point five zero dollars per plate applies to lost or destroyed plates.

lines.text: Notice of Sale within thirty days.
Lost or destroyed: must replace.
Stolen: processing fee, twice a year.

narration.text: To close, put the two situations side by side. When you sell a motor vehicle or all-terrain vehicle, report it with a Notice of Sale, Form five thousand forty-nine, within thirty days, at any license office or by mail to the address on the form. When plates, tabs or a title are lost or destroyed, you are required to apply for a replacement, at eight point five zero dollars for the title, each plate or a set of tabs, plus the nine point zero zero dollars processing fee. When plates and tabs are stolen, a notarized affidavit lets you replace them for only the processing fee, and that free replacement is limited to two times per year.
